svg.aria-label: Choosing between Azure virtual network peering, VPN Gateway and ExpressRoute: the two questions that decide, each product's defining verb, the three cost shapes, sizing and resiliency, and how the three coexist
svg.title: Peering, VPN Gateway or ExpressRoute: two questions eliminate two of the three, and the three charge for different categories of thing rather than different amounts
svg.text: Two questions decide it — then the cost shapes differ in kind, not in amount
THE TWO QUESTIONS THAT ACTUALLY DECIDE
1. What are you joining?
Peering joins Azure VNets to each other and nothing else.
The other two are built to reach outside Azure.
2. May it cross the
public internet?
VPN Gateway’s own description is traffic
over the public Internet. ExpressRoute connections don’t go over it.
A third question can override both: overlapping address space rules peering out at any price.
THREE DEFINING VERBS
PEERING
routes privately between VNets. No bandwidth restriction, local or global
— the VM is the only limit. Not transitive.
VPN GATEWAY
sends ENCRYPTED IPsec/IKE traffic. Site-to-site, point-to-site over
OpenVPN/IKEv2/SSTP, VNet-to-VNet. All tunnels share the gateway’s bandwidth.
EXPRESSROUTE
extends on-prem over a PRIVATE connection, via a connectivity provider, using BGP.
THREE COST SHAPES — NOT THREE PRICES
STANDING COST
DATA COST
Peering
none
ingress AND egress — both directions
VPN Gateway
hourly, per SKU
egress only — and FREE between VNets in one region
ExpressRoute
monthly port
unlimited: all in and out free. metered: in free, out per GB
So for two VNets in ONE region there is a crossover: peering is cheaper at low volume because it has no
standing cost, and a gateway can be cheaper at high volume because its in-region data is free.
The Local SKU folds data transfer into the ExpressRoute port charge. Active-active VPN costs the same as active-passive.
Global Reach sells you transit between your own buildings across the Microsoft network.
SIZING AND RESILIENCY
ExpressRoute circuits
ExpressRoute Direct: dual 10, 100 or 400 Gbps. Resizable in place.
Every circuit has two connections to two MSEEs; dual BGP is required.
Maximum resiliency = TWO circuits in TWO peering locations.
The secondary is not guaranteed for sustained extra traffic — oversubscribing drops packets.
VPN gateway SKUs
Basic: 100 Mbps, 10 tunnels, 200 VMs, no BGP, not zone-redundant.
VpnGw5AZ (Gen2): 10 Gbps, 100 tunnels, 10000 P2S, 9000 VMs, BGP, zonal.
Past 100 site-to-site tunnels, Microsoft sends you to Virtual WAN.
VpnGw1–5 are slated for migration and should not be used for new gateways.
The supported-VM column counts everything that talks THROUGH the gateway — peered spokes, private
endpoints, appliances and PaaS backends. In a hub, that is the whole estate, not the hub’s own VNet.
THEY COEXIST BY DESIGN
· A site-to-site VPN is a documented secure failover path for ExpressRoute.
· A site-to-site VPN reaches the sites ExpressRoute does not — branches that cannot justify a circuit.
· Where a peering AND a gateway join the same pair, traffic uses the peering. The gateway still bills.
Reach is geopolitical before it is global: Premium crosses geopolitical boundaries, lifts private-peering routes 4,000 → 10,000, and VNet links past 10.
And Microsoft’s own advice is that Microsoft 365 was built for the internet — ExpressRoute for it is recommended only for specific scenarios.
